You do understand difference between runtime and build time, correct? Build time code runs when you do `nuxt build` and runtime code runs when you do `nuxt preview` (or `node .output/server/index.mjs`). This issue is about the latter, not the former.

issues.title: Support for unified trailing slash handling
issues.body:
### Describe the feature

Yes, here we go again. I'd like to propose uniform trailing slash handling - as I did [for Nuxt 2](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt.js/pull/6331) - again. But I firmly believe that the implementation can be better, less error prone and even easier with Nuxt 3.

## Why?

Trailing slash handling is crucial when it comes to SEO. Right now, the content shown for `/my-route` and `/my-route/` is already the same. But ideally, one of these versions should not exist (and instead redirect to the other). If that is not possible, a fitting `canonical` URL should be set to define the preferred URL.

Now it seems that it is rather easy, we could go and simply use the `pages:extend` hook and apply/remove the trailing slash and add some nitro page rules (or a middleware) for redirects.

But there is another important part: **the internal linking**.  Often neglected, it **is key for a good on-page SEO**. Ideally, the implementation of this feature would cover correct internal linking too. Ideally, also working with any module, like the `i18n` module.

## Proposal

1. Have a global option to enforce a trailling slash `/route/` or *no* slash `/route` for every internal Nuxt route that exists, ideally including Nitro server-routes (API routes are not that important in this case)
2. The "disallowed" version should redirect to the correct version
3. `<NuxtLink>` should be aware of this choice and adapt linking correctly so the preferred version is the one that will be rendered.

### Additional information

- [X] Would you be willing to help implement this feature?
- [X] Could this feature be implemented as a module?

### Final checks

- [X] Read the [contribution guide](https://v3.nuxtjs.org/community/contribution).
- [X] Check existing [discussions](https://github.com/nuxt/framework/discussions) and [issues](https://github.com/nuxt/framework/issues).

It's one of the reasons I built a few of the submodules in https://github.com/harlan-zw/nuxt-seo-kit. 

Some of the things that require it:
- sitemap
- schema.org
- robots
- canonical urls
- link checking

I was going to add a custom NuxtLink component but I thought the DX of having to use a different link component wasn't worth it, so would be great to see it in the core. It's not a big issue though as the canonical URL fixes any SEO penalties for having both used internally.

## Config

The way I've implemented it in Nuxt SEO Kit was a public runtime called `trailingSlash`. I feel quite strongly that the config should be easily accessible to modules and end users. 

A minor issue is that this is not a convention, I don't think there is any other Nuxt core config within the runtime config?

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  runtimeConfig: {
    public: {
      trailingSlash: true,

})
```

## Middleware

The only issue here is that it won't work in SPA mode. Then the user should redirect using their host or they should set up a canonical URL (this can't be done automatically without having a user-specified site url).

## Other SEO config

This leads to a bigger item which is, adding a Nuxt core config for the site url, which would let us solve a lot of these SEO-related items as part of the core. A much bigger item that would potentially need nitro preset integration, so ignore it for now :P

comments.author: Aareksio
comments.body:
@manniL This issue should probably remain open, given there are scenarios not covered by the plan laid out in [your comment](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/15462#issuecomment-1418944206). I have tried to understand why `trailingSlash` as a nuxt setting is desirable, here are the issues:
1. processing _invalid_ user input
2. prefered version of URL is not enforced
3. module accessing or modifying routes

Examples of invalid user input (against `trailingSlash: 'append'`):
- `<nuxt-link to="/dashboard"/>`
- `navigateTo('/user/1')`
- `defineBreadcrumb({ itemListElement: [{ name: 'Blog', item: '/blog' }] })`

Examples of functionalities misbehaving when one version is not enforced, despite configured `NuxtLink` and the URL leaks:
- canonical URL - one real page becomes two
- schema-org - propagates undesired, duplicated URLs, eg. `/product/1`
- i18n alternate - propagates undesired, duplicated URLs, eg. `/pl/feed`

Examples of modules operating on nuxt generated routes, outputing undesired results:
- sitemap
- robots.txt

---

Invalid input is tricky, the `NuxtLink` supports correcting the user input, but programatic navigation does not. Modules may also require user-provided path, eg. breadcrumb. It should at least be consistent across built-in features (`NuxtLink`, `navigateTo`), currently the `NuxtLink` gets special treatment.

When enforcing only the preferred URL, a lot of modules should work correctly. For example, both schema-org and i18n should base their tags on current URL, which already used the preferred trailing slash setting. And page with other than preferred trailing slash scheme is inaccessible. User can still declare invalid path (eg. `defineBreadcrumb({ itemListElement: [{ name: 'Blog', item: '/blog' }] })`), but the built in resolution should work (eg. `alternate = locales.map((locale) => localePath(currentPath, locale))`).

Finally, we arrive at the biggest issue. Currently there is no way to determine whether `pages/dashboard.vue` is intended to be served as `/dashboard` or `/dashboard/`. This creates a problem for any module trying to list pages for external use, such as sitemap or robots.txt. I do not see any obvious workaround for this right now.

comments.author: gmenunes
comments.body:
> @manniL Partially. Each module can define their options, thus `nuxtseo`, `i18n` or any other module may add own logic to handle the paths. Such logic can be [buggy](https://github.com/nuxt-modules/i18n/issues/1856#issuecomment-1430101572), [hard to discover](https://github.com/nuxt-modules/i18n/issues/1747#issuecomment-1358015273) or not implemented at all. I would not take for granted the fact that 2 of the example modules are maintained by single person who figured sharing the setting is beneficial. Without official recommendation, it **not guaranteed** to be adopted by others. If the modules were independent (there may be better alternative), we end up with:
> 
> ```ts
> // nuxt.conifg.ts
> export default defineNuxtConfig({
>   // ...
>   experimental: { defaults: { nuxtLink: { trailingSlash: 'append' } } },
>   sitemap: { trailingSlash: true },
>   robots: { trailingSlash: true },
>   canonical: { trailingSlash: true },
>   i18n: { trailingSlash: 'append' },
>   // ...
> })
> ```
> 
> Did you notice missing schema-org config? The developer who wrote this code had not, now he deals with angry SEO department raising alarm seeing millions of invalid URLs flood the search index.
> 
> @harlan-zw done a very good job unifying the `trailingSlash` under `site-config-module`, even going as far as allowing user to [skip setting `NuxtLink` default](https://github.com/harlan-zw/nuxt-seo/blob/cd3e7243cbb5a84b44bf63ab003930d1aad90d0f/src/module.ts#L132) and only configure site-config value when using nuxt-seo-kit. Other modules can [opt-in](https://github.com/nuxt-modules/i18n/issues/2474) into this community solution. What I am advocating for is to consider `trailingSlash` as the same kind of configuration as [siteUrl](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/18808) in Nuxt.

Thank you, these settings helped a ton!
But once we add them, our production build takes more than 25min. After reverting it takes 5 min or so.

Feedback and suggestions are welcome! > [!IMPORTANT] > Website pages classed as redirects might not be indexed by Search Engines e.g. Google, Bing etc. therefore users may not find your site. > [!TIP] > This comment contains terms such as **CSR**, **SSR**, **SSG**, **Universal rendering**. > Learn more about the terms at [Rendering Modes · Nuxt Concepts](https://nuxt.com/docs/guide/concepts/rendering). ### Walkthrough example: SSG Site pages not indexing
Details

In this example Nuxt site is generated with **Server Side Generation** (SSG) mode with **Universal rendering**. Read [Rendering Modes · Nuxt Concepts](https://nuxt.com/docs/guide/concepts/rendering) for descriptions of the other modes. The site is configured to link to pages without trailing slashes. The site uses a sitemap with path contents: - `/` - `/hello` The canonical path tag on each page matches the sitemap. #### Environment: Development Developer uses `dev` version of site **SSR** + **CSR**: - Pages align with sitemap and canonical tags ```bash pnpm dev ``` |CSR path|web server resolved path|Canonical path|Sitemap path|All paths match| |-|-|-|-|-| |/ | / | / | / | ✅ | |/hello|/hello|/hello|/hello|✅| #### Environment: Preview Developer uses `preview` version of site: ```bash pnpm generate ``` ```bash pnpm preview ``` |CSR path|Web server resolved path|Canonical path|Sitemap path|All paths match| |-|-|-|-|-| |/ | / | / | / | ✅ | |/hello|/hello|/hello|/hello|✅| > Underlying Web Server: [serve](https://www.npmjs.com/package/serve) #### Environment: Production Using any of the following static html servers: - [Cloudflare Pages](https://pages.cloudflare.com/) - Local testing with: ```bash pnpm dlx wrangler pages dev ``` - [NGINX](https://nginx.org/en/) - [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com/) |CSR path|web server resolved path|Canonical path|Sitemap path|All paths match| |-|-|-|-|-| |/ | / | / | / | ✅ | |/hello| /hello/ |/hello|/hello|❌| All paths do not match as the web server for the request `/hello` returns a redirect instead of the page contents. Therefore the CSR path does not match the Nuxt route. ###### Production Search Engine indexing example > [!NOTE] > When the diagram loads, the scroll position on this GitHub page position may shift.

### Potential SSG solution without trailing slashes > [!WARNING] > Use these potential workaround solutions at your own risk. No warranties or guarantees are provided.
Details

#### Cloudflare ##### Solution If using Cloudflare Pages follow those instructions instead. ##### Hotfix This hotfix use path rewrites to mimic the functionality of the Nuxt preview command. It is only recommended as a last resort. Updating the config in the Nuxt deployment or web server is preferred over using a proxy server (Cloudflare).

Details

Follow the instructions below to create a Transform Rule to alter the requested path to the origin server. In the [Cloudflare Dashboard](https://dash.cloudflare.com/) > [Select Account] > [Select Domain] > Rules > Transform Rules > Rewrite URL ##### Custom filter expression ###### If incoming requests match… Click **Edit expression**: ``` (starts_with(http.request.uri.path, "/") and not ends_with(http.request.uri.path, "/") and not http.request.uri.path contains "." and not starts_with(http.request.uri.path, "/_nuxt/") and not starts_with(http.request.uri.path, "/api/") and http.host eq "example.com") ``` Click **Use expression builder** > Replace `example.com` with your domain. > Ensure you add any non page directories from your build e.g. `/_ipx/` `/images/` > If your pages contain the `.` character consider excluding file extension instead. Use, ends with matching and values such as `.txt`, `.xml`, `.html`. ##### Then… | Set Rewrite parameters | Path | **Rewrite to...** **Dynamic** ``` wildcard_replace(http.request.uri.path, r"/*", r"/${1}/") ``` ##### Nuxt Ensure your pages include a [canonical tag](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) to inform search engines which version is the primary page.

#### Cloudflare Pages
Details

Follow the [Route matching | Deploy Nuxt to Cloudflare](https://nuxt.com/deploy/cloudflare#route-matching) instructions. Update Nuxt config to include the nitro option `autoSubfolderIndex` to `false`: ```ts export default defineNuxtConfig({ nitro: { prerender: { autoSubfolderIndex: false } } }) ```

#### Nginx No NGINX fix is available as this time. Consider using a proxy service like Cloudflare, using the Cloudflare instructions. Note use `try_files $uri $uri/index.html;` may result in an internal redirection loop for non matching files. #### Caddy
Details

Follow the instructions. Update Nuxt config to include the nitro option `autoSubfolderIndex` to `false`: ```ts export default defineNuxtConfig({ nitro: { prerender: { autoSubfolderIndex: false } } }) For more information on what `autoSubfolderIndex` does, read the [Route matching | Deploy Nuxt to Cloudflare](https://nuxt.com/deploy/cloudflare#route-matching). Update your `Caddyfile` to use the `autoSubfolderIndex` route matching. `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`: ```diff :80 { # Set this path to your site's directory. root * /usr/share/caddy # Enable the static file server. file_server + # Add fallback for path /hello to file /hello.html + try_files {path} {path}.html # Another common task is to set up a reverse proxy: # reverse_proxy localhost:8080 # Or serve a PHP site through php-fpm: # php_fastcgi localhost:9000 } ``` > Remove `+` symbol when copying Reload the server with: ```bash caddy reload --adapter caddyfile --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile ```

### Potential SSG workaround solution with trailing slashes > [!WARNING] > Use these potential workaround solutions at your own risk. No warranties or guarantees are provided.
Details

Use-case scenario: - Using SSG with universal rendering - Want all pages to have trailing slashes - Want pages to be indexed by search engines In `nuxt.config.ts` ```ts // https://nuxt.com/docs/api/configuration/nuxt-config export default defineNuxtConfig({ experimental: { defaults: { nuxtLink: { // Ensure linking uses trailing slash trailingSlash: 'append' } } }, hooks: { // any other hooks // Ensure page trailing slash "pages:extend"(pages) { for (const page of pages) { page.path = page.path.endsWith("/") ? page.path : page.path + "/"; } }, }, // The rest of your Nuxt config ``` Thanks to @gmenunes for the example hooks code in https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/15462#issuecomment-2011782964, @harlan-zw and the [NuxtLink · Nuxt Components](https://nuxt.com/docs/api/components/nuxt-link#overwriting-defaults) documentation. Make sure to update your sitemap and canonical URLS to ensure they match and have a trailing slash.

comments.author: IO-Fire
comments.body:
Also noteworthy, is that the [nuxt.com](https://nuxt.com/) website and many more, serve duplicate content with a trailing slash instead of a redirect:

```curl -I 'https://nuxt.com/docs/getting-started/installation/'``` returns HTTP `200` and uses a CSR redirect. This highlights the importance of using a [canonical tag](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) to inform search engines which is the preferred URL.

Not using a redirect may needless consume extra crawl budget as the page has to be parsed and rendered.

> [!NOTE]
>  `https://nuxt.com/docs/getting-started/installation` does not include a canonical tag, including it can help ensure web crawlers choose the correct URL for the page.

> [!WARNING]
> If you are including a [canonical tag](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls), ensure this is the address of the page and it is not a redirect. Use cURL to test the deployed page, CSR redirects are easily missed.

I propose that CSR redirects are not a recommended solution to updating the path. HTTP redirects would be preferred. 

Anecdotal evidence suggests that CSR redirects also impact [lighthouse](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/) scores.

```ts
// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  modules: ['nuxt-github-pages']
})
```

That's it! The module automatically creates duplicate HTML files during build to ensure both `/path` and `/path/` work correctly on GitHub Pages.

## What it does

- For every `/path/to/page/index.html`, it creates `/path/to/page.html`
- Zero configuration required
- Works with both GitHub Pages and Netlify
- No runtime overhead - it's purely a build-time solution

## Resources

- **npm**: https://www.npmjs.com/package/nuxt-github-pages
- **GitHub**: https://github.com/mitre/nuxt-github-pages
- **Detailed explanation & alternatives**: https://gist.github.com/aaronlippold/ddf912495a9656b115a1d1735569ff99

While we wait for a proper solution in Nuxt core, this module provides a battle-tested fix that's already in production use. Hope this helps! 🚀

Hi @danielroe and team\! 

I wanted to follow up on the SEO duplicate content concern raised here. We've addressed this in the `nuxt-github-pages` module:

### Solution Implemented (v1.1.0+)

The module now automatically injects canonical URLs to prevent duplicate content issues:

```html
<\!-- Both /about and /about/index.html will have: -->

```

### Features:
- 🔍 **Automatic canonical URL injection** (enabled by default)
- 🎯 **Configurable trailing slashes** via `trailingSlash` option
- 🚫 **Can be disabled** via `canonicalUrls: false` if needed
- ✅ **Both files point to the same canonical URL**, telling search engines which version is preferred

issues.title: Allow modules / layers to use auto-imports in nitro context
issues.body:
## Problem

Imagine you're developing a module and you have some nitro code like this:

```ts
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  // do something
})
```

When working on a module locally, this works fine. The `defineEventHandler` import is auto-imported.

However, when deploying this code, the auto-imports no longer work. This is due to `node_modules` being excluded from nitro's unimport config.

See: https://github.com/unjs/nitro/blob/main/src/options.ts#L47

This means the module author has to import explicitly otherwise the end-user will get errors. This has a few issues:
- Inconsistent behavior. Local development works, also module components / composables can use `#import`
- Nitro imports aren't typed (could be an IDE issue)

For example, I spent quite a while trying to figure out how to import `getRouteRules`.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5326365/207766353-08113358-a774-4155-91ca-8e4ff6800386.png)

I haven't tested it, but I feel like this will also be a problem for layers.

## Proposed Solution

Ideally, all of the module paths would be included for auto-import scanning.

This would probably require removing node_modules from the exclude, as I think this takes priority over the includes. (needs further testing)

Happy to look into creating a PR if you agree this should be the behavior.

## Hacky solution

```ts
 hooks: {
    'nitro:init'(nitro) {
      // prev [/[/\\]node_modules[/\\]/, /[/\\]\.git[/\\]/],
      nitro.options.imports.exclude = [/[/\\]\.git[/\\]/]
    }
  },
```

### Additional information

- [X] Would you be willing to help implement this feature?
- [ ] Could this feature be implemented as a module?

### Final checks

- [X] Read the [contribution guide](https://v3.nuxtjs.org/community/contribution).
- [X] Check existing [discussions](https://github.com/nuxt/framework/discussions) and [issues](https://github.com/nuxt/framework/issues).

Hey @silverbackdan I just ran into a similar issue and discovered a solution [here](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/14245#issuecomment-1397351583) → which leads to [here](https://github.com/sppmstar/nuxt-3-module-layout-vite-bug/blob/125de3c9545f7fd8a52e1da0dc315c93113614ab/src/module.ts#L23-L25) for some sample code. This did it for me :)

```js
import { createResolver, addTemplate, addLayout } from '@nuxt/kit'

const { resolve } = createResolver(import.meta.url)

---

const template = addTemplate({
  src: resolve('runtime/layouts/new-layout.vue'),
  write: true
})

addLayout(template, 'my-fancy-layout') // the 2nd argument (String) is where you define the layout slug to be passed into definePageMeta
```

comments.author: silverbackdan

comments.body:
The issue here seems to be that `@vitejs/plugin-vue` does not support virtual `.vue` files.

A workaround is to add `write: true` to the first argument passed to `addLayout`, as you spotted.

```diff
  addLayout({
+   write: true
    src: resolve(vueTemplatesDir, 'layouts', 'cwa-default.vue'),
    filename: join('cwa', 'layouts', 'cwa-default.vue')
  }, 'cwa-default')
```

issues.title: Allow sharing app config with build-time modules
issues.body:
### Describe the feature

Hi :wave: , 
It would be nice to be able to use `useAppConfig` within modules since this can be used by modules to get non-stringifyable data in plugins. 

Currently there's like a dependency loop when we import an `app.config.ts` (in a module file) with 

````ts
import { defineAppConfig } from "nuxt/app"
export default defineAppConfig({ /* ..... */  })
````
if we don't specify the import, the import will fail since `app.config.ts` has not been transformed.

using `useAppConfig()` in modules triggers the same issue since it need to be imported from `nuxt/app`

### Additional information

- [ ] Would you be willing to help implement this feature?
- [ ] Could this feature be implemented as a module?

### Final checks

comments.body:
this is linked to https://github.com/huang-julien/nuxt-runtime-compiler/pull/37, https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/15553 and https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/discussions/18413. 

What i'm trying to do is to use `app.config.ts` to define the `compilerOptions` for vue in runtime through a plugin. However since this is only applied to vue in runtime, I would like to pass theses options, more specifically the `isCustomElementTag` function from the app.config to the nuxt config at build time. this would avoid to define the `compileroptions` twice.

Importing from `#app` or `#imports` within the module fails and I think most of the users won't import it since it is auto-imported.

comments.author: danielroe
comments.body:
This is tricky - `app.config` is specifically meant to allow runtime code that relies on the entire Nuxt app context and importing or relying on it in the build-time part of modules is I think not something we can easily support.

This would be fine for anything that's serialisable - you could just set it in module options. But I recognise that (for example) functions are not so easy.

comments.author: danielroe
comments.body:
I think we would find it difficult to support this, but maybe we it would be worth gradually adopting a single location for shared config between build/runtime that module authors can use. e.g. module author can read in a `~/config/my-module.mjs` file which will be accessible at build time within module as well as imported by module in build.

A docs PR might be worth it to the module authors guide.

issues.title: Components automatically injected into the root element
issues.body: ### Describe the feature Sometimes you need to have multiple components in the `app.vue` file, or as close to the root element as possible. For example, if you have multiple modals that must be present not only on every page, but also on every layout (dialogs, cookie notice, etc) or any other interface resource and you must add each one manually somewhere in the `app.vue` file. I think it would be nice to have a directory for "universal" components that Nuxt detects and automatically injects into the root element. This would perfectly follow the philosophy of the framework to improve the DX as much as possible. An example of how it would be now and how it could be: ```vue // ~/app.vue ``` Or you could just move those components to a directory called `~/components/universal` (for example) and Nuxt would take care of injecting them automatically. ### Additional information - [X] Would you be willing to help implement this feature? - [ ] Could this feature be implemented as a module? ### Final checks - [X] Read the [contribution guide](https://nuxt.com/docs/community/contribution). - [X] Check existing [discussions](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/discussions) and [issues](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues).
issues.author: imlautaro

comments.author: AloisSeckar
comments.body:
I would find a good use for that in my project, but I have a couple of questions/concerns/remarks:

1. Is that even a good pattern to have a bunch of components, mostly modal windows I guess, like that? I mean, I came up with the very same solution to handle modals in my apps, but somehow I dont like it, especially as the number of such components tends to grow as the project grows... 
2. If yes, they can still quite easilly be wrapped in a dedicated component and the problem is gone. Or?
3. It adds a new level of complexity, because you should be aware that this new special directory exits and behaves differently than "normal" `components`. So are the potential benefits really worth it?
4. If my previous point is correct - ain't that rather a use case for a new module or plugin? Because some people may benefit from it, while others won't. 

Please don't take it like I want to mock or destroy your idea. This is just what came up my mind right now.

comments.author: imlautaro
comments.body:
First of all, thanks for the feedback! I'll tell you what I think about each point you mention:

1. This feature in Nuxt by default would precisely allow the code to follow a more logical structure and a better pattern, because at the end of the day in relatively large projects you will always need UI elements that are available in every route and layout, so instead of having to manually add them to the `app.vue` file where those components have no relationship with each other and do not share a state, it would make more sense for them to be in a universal folder and for Nuxt to inject them in the background.
2. Yes, you can safely place each component inside a dedicated one, but we would have the same "hassle" of having to add a bunch of unrelated components to the same file just so they can be in the app.
3. Regarding the complexity, I don't think it is harmful in the least, I think it would be somewhat intuitive to have these components in a dedicated folder as well as we have the global components and in the case of nuxt content the components to use in the MDC . It could also be seen as what we already have with middlewares, where we can add the .global extension so they are automatically injected into each route. It would be pretty much the same applied to components, only in this case I think a directory makes more sense than using a .univeral.vue extension for example.
4. Finally, regarding this point I think it could be implemented as a feature within the nuxt package and if someone doesn't need this functionality, they simply don't use it and that doesn't interfere or overload anything else.

In short, I think it would be an intuitive feature that could improve the development experience for those who need it without annoying those who don't. So, let me know what you think and let's await for the Nuxt team to tell us what they think as well 😄

issues.title: server component roadmap
issues.body:
We have experimental support in Nuxt 3 for both island components and server-only components (which are implemented using islands) - see https://github.com/nuxt/framework/pull/5689 and https://github.com/nuxt/framework/pull/9972 for initial implementations and https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/discussions/17956 for initial partial RFC.

There are a number of future linked improvements. This issue is to track those and provide some place to document the linking story, purpose and usage of server components within Nuxt.

## Purpose and usage

Currently we are collecting use patterns to ensure that the final API and implementation for server components is useful. But the following are some benefits we are exploring:

1. security and direct access to server APIs within certain components
2. separate caching strategies for individual chunks of HTML
3. leaner bundle size (keeping some dependencies solely on the server, e.g. syntax highlighting)
4. extensibility
5. rendering individual components within other modules or server routes (e.g. for component previews, OG images, PDF downloads, etc.)
6. ...

Comments and suggestions are very welcome.

- [x] Allow async components - https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/18500
- [x] Client-side interactivity - https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/19765
- [x] remove server component content from payload and prefetch on route transition: https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/pull/21461
- [x] Hybrid/remote/streaming sources for server components - https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/12343
- [x] lazy (non-blocking) server components
- [x] interactive components within server components
- [x] deep interactive components within server components
- [x] slot refactor to stabilize the API for other remotes sources such as CMS
- [x] server pages
- [ ] A deep documentation for islands: https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/pull/35778
- [ ] Looking for server-side Performance optimisation opportunity
- [ ] Apply islands features to non SFC components
issues.author: danielroe

comments.author: Twitch0125
comments.body: I think it'd make sense to have all the available auto imports for server route handlers be available for server components.

comments.author: Hebilicious
comments.body:
This looks promising. Here's my personal 2 cents for "server components".

_Disclaimer: I think this name in general is extremely confusing, due to the fact that it's already complicated to understand what's going on. This is not really a problem related to Nuxt, but React has the same problem with RSC, where most people don't really know how they differ from SSR components... Anyways here is some [reading](https://www.plasmic.app/blog/how-react-server-components-work) to get up to speed ... ._

## 1) More Unified Rendering API

Right now here's a recap of what is possible (correct me if I'm wrong) :

- Nitro [route rules](https://nitro.unjs.io/guide/routing) : It is possible to decide where and how a *page* will be rendered. This also allows the handling of more things, like caching rules, redirect, headers ... 
  - This works at the page level through a config file
  - This allows patterns like SPA/SSG/SSR/SSR+SWR
  
- Nuxt [Server components](https://nuxt.com/docs/guide/directory-structure/components#server-components) : It is possible to tag a *component* as server only by using `.server.vue`. This disable hydration and achieve the same thing as SSG.
  - Works at the component level through the file name
  - This allows pattern like "0 javascript" components.

- Nuxt [Client components](https://nuxt.com/docs/guide/directory-structure/components#clientonly-component) : This is a vue component that can be used to disable SSR at the *component* level, using a wrapper component.
  - Works at the component level through a wrapper component
  - This allows patterns like "Javascript only" rendering.

As we add more and more features and new things, this becomes hard to understand what takes priority and how everything works. I'm not sure what would be a good way to unify everything. That being said, given that routes and pages are also components, I would personally like to have a good granular API that works for both: 

```vue
// This could be "aliased" to nuxt="server" and further down to "nuxt-server"
<script setup nuxt="{ render: 'server', hydrate: false }">
console.log("This will be logged on the server only")
</script>
<template>Server Only</template>
```

```vue
// This could be "aliased" to nuxt="client" and further down "nuxt-client"
<script setup nuxt="{ render: 'client' }">
console.log("This will be logged on the client only")
</script>
<template>Client Only</template>
```

This would be compatible with the "naming" api, ie, renaming a file to `.server.vue` would effectively do the same as using the nuxt="server" script tag. `<ClientOnly />` could be deprecated and replaced by `.client.vue`. 

There could be a configuration file/hook to define custom rendering "templates" so they can be re-used easily (like nuxt="server" => nuxt="{ render:'server', hydrate: false}"). 

If I'm not mistaken the default for all components and pages should be nuxt="{ render:'server', hydrate: 'true' }" and therefore can be omitted. There should be an easy way to change this default, to enable full SPA or SSG by default. 

This is meant to work in tandem with Nitro and these should be "merged" with route rules (the same keys can be used in both route rules and here to unify the API). Some kind of human-readable auto-generated artifact (`nuxt-rendered.json` ?) should be generated, representing the component tree, so there's a source of truth of what's going on. This can be used by VSCode extensions and the likes for more advanced use case, such as displaying a different file icon for server/client components...

We can detect the "invalid" configurations (ie render: "client" + prerender: "true" or hydrate: "true") and emit a warning.

### Alternative API

A few other alternatives API are worth suggesting :

```vue
//could be nuxt-render etc
<render>
export { render: 'server', hydrate: false, prerender: true }
</render>
<script setup>console.log("full static")</script>
```

```vue
<script setup>
useNuxtRender(() => ({render: "server", hydrate: "false"}))
console.log("server Only")
</script>
```

## 2) "Hybrid Component tree" and Streaming

Currently RSC can support a tree like this (we can achieve something similar with slots)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13395944/233835114-b378f01e-5f9f-4376-9b4c-b690b39ed9f9.png)
The entire tree is passed as JSON, and the client side code can reconstruct it with references to the client only components.
So maybe the [RFC here](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/discussions/17956) needs to be extended to handle all use-cases ?

The streaming part can be a little confusing, we definitely need better naming conventions... 
I know that there's some plans regarding streaming, and I wrote this in [another issue](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/4753#issuecomment-1502117379), and this might be off-topic. Now that Lambda supports streaming, as well as Cloudflare Workers, how does this relate to Server Component streaming is an interesting question. They are different, as the HTML streaming is something related to the way the server sends HTML to the client, while the server component streaming is JSON based api-communication.

What I would assume is that if we have some kind of nested layout like this : 

```
+------+------------------------------------+
| Index                                     |
|      +------+-----------------------------+
|      | SSG                                |
|      |      +------+----------------------+
|      |      | ServerOnly                  |
|      |      +-----------------------------+
|      +------------------------------------+
+------+------------------------------------+
```
Here Nuxt could use both HTML streaming (using vue pipeToWebWritable instead of renderToString), to send what's already present on the server (static layouts, pre-rendered pages/components), and then execute the the ServerOnly component rendering and pass that to the client using ... a different "stream" ?

Now I don't know if this different stream is what you meant by "Hybrid/remote/streaming sources for server components".

Note that for React, the Root component needs to be a "server component", and that server components supports children (ie slots) that can be either client or server components.

## 3) Nuxt Islands and relation to @vue/core

*I'm not very familiar with that part of the code*

The current implementation looks a little like this right now : the current server components use `createStaticVNode`/`createStaticVNode` and raw html from an internal nitro endpoint to render server components on the client. 
The Nitro endpoint use `renderToString`, then respond with an object that contains the serialised html and the state (payload). That payload is then "revived" on the client side.

Perhaps this revive logic should be handled by Vue and not by Nuxt. I'm not sure what the benefits would be or if that's something that isn't priority, but it's worth mentioning here. Maybe the vue renderer should have this functionality and should be able to "revive" the state, but also event listeners, lifecycle hooks and everything else that is needed.

### Describe the feature

I think it is a common use case (at least I have it a lot) that you want to have some side effects when navigating via NuxtLink that need to wait until the navigation is complete, e.g. if you have a link in a menu or dropdown that should close when clicking the link. A simple solution would be the following:

```vue
<NuxtLink

  title="Some page"
  @navigation-complete="closeMenu()"
/>
```

I think implementation should be simple. In the NuxtLink component we would just need to do

```ts
navigateTo(...)
  // New:
  .then(emit('navigationComplete', to))
```

I guess???

Hey @septatrix 👋 

Thanks for the issue - don't have a direct enhancement proposal to Nuxt itself, but here's two things you can already do that have solved this for me in the past:
- Create a server plugin, in the plugin do the seeding. You can ensure that it only runs once by checking if the database already contains data before seeding
- Create a module that does the seeding for you. Import and run itninside the nuxt.config.ts. This can be arbitrarily expanded, e.g., you could run this only when certain environment variables are there or when certain args are passed

comments.author: AaronBeaudoin
comments.body:
I think that moving this into Nuxt core would be very smart. **Nuxt maintainers**—If you have not already read this article, please check it out for why this feature is arguably such a significant steps forward:

> [**The Web’s Next Transition**](https://www.epicweb.dev/the-webs-next-transition) — Kent C. Dodds
> _Progressively Enhanced Single Page Apps (PESPAs)_

**TLDR**: Form actions not only provide the benefit of a built-in way to allow a website to work even in the absence of JavaScript (see [this](https://www.kryogenix.org/code/browser/everyonehasjs.html) commonly linked flowchart), but more importantly, they allow for a dramatically simpler mental model by simplifying state management and colocating related client and server code.

Also, interest in this approach is gaining traction with both [Next.js 14](https://nextjs.org/blog/next-14#server-actions-stable) getting _Server Actions_ as of Oct 26 which can be used with forms for progressive enhancement and [Remix](https://remix.run/blog/remix-heart-vite) getting Vite support as of Oct 31 which should help it's adoption. Notably, [SvelteKit](https://kit.svelte.dev/docs/routing#server-receiving-data) mentions in its docs that although API routes can be used to send data to the server, form actions "are a better way to submit data".

Sematically, Nuxt already does the equivalent of this for `<a>` elements. Before JS loads, the browser default behavior simply works as a "fallback", but after JavaScript loads (or potentially **_if_** it loads) then client-side navigation is used and the links are "progressively enhanced". This feature would just extends that philosophy to `<form>` elements, which is extremely powerful for DX and accessibility.

issues.title: Throwing an error in a server route causes an infinite loop when fetched inside a server only plugin
issues.body: ### Environment - Operating System: `Darwin` - Node Version: `v18.16.0` - Nuxt Version: `3.5.0` - Nitro Version: `2.4.1` - Package Manager: `pnpm@8.5.0` - Builder: `vite` - User Config: `-` - Runtime Modules: `-` - Build Modules: `-` ### Reproduction https://stackblitz.com/edit/github-v83zpl-v8bzgm ### Describe the bug When I fetch a server route endpoint `server/routes/****.get.ts` inside a server plugin `plugins/****.server.ts`, **if the server route throws an error, it causes an infinite loop**, calling the the plugin and fetching data from the server route again and again. ### Additional context It does not happen if its an api server route `server/api/****.get.ts` or inside a client plugin `plugins/****.client.ts`. Catching the error inside the server plugin does not prevent this behaviour : ```ts try { await $fetch('/hello'); } catch (error) { console.error(error); } ``` ### Logs _No response_
issues.author: damien-hl

comments.author: danielroe
comments.body:
Yes. The issue is that in order to render the _error page_ (being returned to `$fetch('/hello')`, Nuxt will use your `error.vue` (or the built-in one) to render an HTML page in your app, and still run all the same plugins... Hence, infinite recursion.

I think we could look to add some kind of detection for this, to improve DX.

comments.author: philippeducasse
comments.body: hi @danielroe , I would like to take over this issue, is it still relevant?

comments.author: stephanelgrg
comments.body:
Hello there, 

**Here is what I understand of this issue:**
When a server-only plugin calls $fetch() for a server route and that route throws, Nuxt would still initialize plugins during the server error render. That caused the plugin to run again while rendering the error response, leading to an infinite recursion loop.

**So my idea would be to:**
- Detect server-side error renders in entry.ts
- Skip applyPlugins(nuxt, plugins) when ssrContext.payload.error or ssrContext.error is present

Do you think, this is the way to solve this? 🙏

comments.author: stephanelgrg
comments.body: Hello 👋 I'm still investigating this issue, and today I found something interesting. In the providing example: the API is in `playground/server/routes/hello.get.ts` causing a loop like this one: **But**, following this doc: https://nuxt.com/docs/4.x/directory-structure/server we can / should declare the endpoint in: `playground/server/api/hello.ts` and it's having a direct impact on this issue: We can see multiple calls, but no loop anymore 👏 ➡️ Direct fix: use /server/api instead of /server/routes ➡️ I'll keep on investigating this slowly 🐌

issues.title: Add "publish" style command to run functions and copy from layers/modules directly into the project
issues.body:
### Describe the feature

It would be very helpful if we had the ability to develop layers or modules for Nuxt which came with a "publish" type of command which could be run by users. This would execute a command in the package which would copy select files from the package into the actual published app.

An example use-case for a feature like this would be to develop something like a layer, but to then publish the pages and components directly into the app's pages or components directories. By copying the content into these folders it allows developers to more easily see the structure of what has been added, but more importantly start making changes to the published files directly. 

We can overwrite content of layers and modules by making our own components and pages which match the package's, but doing that for a significant number of things requires digging into the package source and manually making your own copies of the files, which can be very time-consuming and error-prone.

This kind of feature is very useful when your package has the expectation that what you're publishing is just a template and will generally require customization. 

An example of this behavior in another platform is with [Laravel Jetstream](https://jetstream.laravel.com/). After installing the Jetstream package you run a publish command to copy the starter template of things like login pages, basic form components, nav menus, and other basic app configurations. The expectation is that you as the developer are going to need to make some significant style, theme, or behavior changes to the starter kit which has been copied into your app by the publish process. Having all of those files there, though, makes it very easy to find things like your login page to start changing your styling and branding.

We'd like to make and publish our own version of something like Jetstream for Nuxt, which would give us a starter-kit to cover things like basic auth, menus, password resets, and some starter database configuration. In our organization we'd be using this as a starting point for a lot of projects for different companies, and they'd each need to have significantly different branding and theming. Having the layer content or select module content actually published into the project would make the process of starting to work on something like this very straightforward.

### Additional information

- [X] Would you be willing to help implement this feature?
- [ ] Could this feature be implemented as a module?

### Final checks

- [X] Read the [contribution guide](https://nuxt.com/docs/community/contribution).
- [X] Check existing [discussions](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/discussions) and [issues](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues).
issues.author: Smef

comments.author: pi0
comments.body: This might be really useful. I think we could support publish/eject functionality with upcoming versions of Nuxi CLi from layers.

comments.author: Hebilicious
Smef
comments.body:
It wouldn't necessarily be the whole contents. Depending on the module and what the package developer thinks the users would care about it might only be a certain subset of files, such as some components, layouts, or configuration files.

Package/module/layer developers may even want to provide people using the package the option to publish or eject certain contents, such as only components and config.

For the example of a starter kit, it would probably want to publish a bunch of components, a config file for the functionality and features, maybe a tailwind config and tsconfig and a couple of other project files.  Things that might not be published might be something like some auth routes or logic. You could still override it if you wanted to, but the package author might decide that it's not worth publishing that by default.

The expectation in this case would be that you're running through this process on a brand new project and that if you aren't for some reason, you're likely to override something in your project with the module's published content.

[Statamic](https://statamic.com/), a CMS, is another example that does something like this as part of an "install" command that you run. When you install Statamic you also "publish" some assets into your main project src. This publish process creates some folders that you'll need, some example files, and some necessary config files. There are still a bunch of files and logic in the package which don't get published, such as a control panel.

Module developers may want to publish everything, but they may also only want to publish a select number of files.

...
...
...

I wrote all this up and then thought was thinking about what an alternative solution would look like. This could be done with an `npx` command from the package. As an example of this, Tailwind has an `npx tailwindcss init` which does some very similar stuff. It publishes some config files as part of an install process.

I think the main difference between this sort of a command and a bit more robust publish type command would be reducing boilerplate that the package developers need to write.
Some examples of saving boilerplate would be:

- Getting paths to specific standard project folders, like the pages directory
- Built-in handling of cases where common folders don't exist yet (again, like a pages directory)
- Standardized handling of file overwrite protection and warnings
- Built-in handling of streaming read/write source to destination files
- Built-in handling for bulk-copying whole directories and subdirectories.

Standardization of this process could make it easier for module developers to get their content into the right place, and would prevent people from needing to include additional packages in their modules just to do some standard file management stuff.

With all this considered it seems like it's all doable currently with an npx command. This would be more of a DX feature or standardization feature than something that would allow us to do things which currently aren't possible at all.

comments.author: Hebilicious
comments.body:
Right, so basically you're suggesting something that would work like this:

- as a module developer you add to some kind of manifest file/config any files that you want to publish/eject.
- you publish your module, these files are added to npm under some kind of special directory in the published package
- the consumer of your module/layers would then run a command and these files would be copied from node_modules to his local directory 
- nuxt.config.ts would get updated 

A couple of things comes to mind :

For modules that don't publish everything then the local version would probably break, so maybe that shouldn't be allowed.
I really think the idea of ejecting a module into its source code would encourage people to contribute back to modules, but that might not work for modules with advanced build steps. Maybe `nuxt-build-module` could test if the module is ejectable and then the `nuxi eject` command would be allowed/disallowed based on that. 

For layers you made a lot of good points, I'm thinking also that if you have relative dependencies in your layers and you don't publish them (ComponentA uses ComponentB and ComponentC, but component C isn't ejected), what should happen when the user ejects?

comments.author: danielroe
comments.body:
I think this would be a great idea!

First steps would be to implement this in a standalone package - either/both:

1) a CLI command (`nuxt-eject` is available) - this will be automatically picked up by nuxi to allow you to run `nuxi eject` and copy layers into your project. I think we might also consider supporting auto-resolution of any files in `~/layers` (cc: @pi0) as layers - though note that this would likely require integration with `c12`.
2) a Nuxt module that exposes an iframe to Nuxt Devtools to allow ejecting via Devtools command

Feel free to ping any of us to help.

comments.author: Smef
comments.body: I think we're going to be working on a starter kit for our company to use to bootstrap projects quickly which we plan to open-source, and this would be a good actual test case for this concept.

comments.author: RaphaelDDL
comments.body:
For visibility on the main tracker for multiApp, a couple experiences with it so far.

### nuxt/test-utils break with multiapp true

Logged the issue in https://github.com/nuxt/test-utils/issues/1521 where `useRouter()` in _node_modules/@nuxt/test-utils/dist/runtime/shared/nuxt.mjs:6:14_ for `page:finish` hook throws when multiApp is true.

The workaround we have for now is to set a `process.env.something = true;` var in vitest.config and use it as the !value in nuxt.config's multiApp. So it's multiapp when building and running, but disabled when running tests.


### Implementation in an app

Layer doesn't work for what we needed, so we went with two apps and multiApp.

Having an app with multiapp true and an app with multiapp false has different behavior depending on order. 

At first we injected the scripts of the multiapp into the nonmultiapp last onto `head` (so the nuxt running the page had no multiapp and the injected having multiapp), and had no conflicts or errors. If you switch the order - injected multiapp first in head, app without multiapp after - then it starts throwing errors in router (`Error matching route rules. TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'entries')` in `_sortRoutesMap` )and got reports of hydration issues too. 

The fix was set multiapp on both, which I assume is the most correct way but found interesting to share since multiapp does not conflict if loaded second. 

In both cases we have the multiApp one using '@rollup/plugin-replace' to change the window namespace to avoid conflicts `replace({  __NUXT__: '__NUXT_APP__', })` as a `nitro.rollupConfig.plugins`.

To be honest, between Layer, multiApp and module federation, if module federation worked in SSR, I believe that would've been the best choice but no idea how fix vite-plugin-federation to work in SSR( https://github.com/originjs/vite-plugin-federation/issues/239 )

comments.author: IlyaSemenov
comments.body:
Just leaving this here in case it helps others following this issue: I published [nuxt-multi-app](https://github.com/IlyaSemenov/nuxt-multi-app), a module that runs multiple independent Nuxt apps behind one server.

It runs each app with its own Nuxt config, modules, routes, styles, assets and generated types, behind one dev server and one production process, with routing by host/path.

This is deliberately **not** client-side microfrontend composition, and is independent from Nuxt core's broader `multiApp` work discussed here. It's a beta, but already usable if this particular flavor of multi-app is what you need.

issues.title: Allow an array of strings for `path` in `definePageMeta`
issues.body:
### Describe the feature

In my project, I have one page that is responsible for many urls.  It would be nice to be able to add multiple routes to the page via definePageMeta.path instead of only one.  Right now, we've had to resort to pushing each route manually via pages:extend hook which fragments the logic for the page into different places.

Example:
/c/exterior-accessories/
/c/exterior-accessories/tonneau-covers/
/c/exterior-accessories/tonneau-covers/v/chevy/
/b/bak/
/specials/
/new-products/v/chevy/
... and more.

being able to add multiple paths in definePageMeta could let us do something like this.
```
definePageMeta({
 path: [
  '/c/:lvl0/:lvl1?/:lvl2?/:lvl3?',
  '/c/:lvl0/:lvl1?/:lvl2?/:lvl3?/v/:makeSlug/:modelSlug?/:year(\\d{4})?',
  '/b/:brandSlug',
  '/b/:brandSlug/v/:makeSlug/:modelSlug?/:year(\\d{4})?'
 ]
})
```

### Additional information

- [ ] Would you be willing to help implement this feature?

issues.title: Nuxt does not clean up CSS after navigation (and injects CSS pre-navigation)
issues.body:
### Environment

- Operating System: `Darwin`
- Node Version:     `v16.19.0`
- Nuxt Version:     `3.6.5`
- Nitro Version:    `2.5.2`
- Package Manager:  `pnpm@8.3.1`
- Builder:          `vite`
- User Config:      `extends`, `srcDir`, `build`, `hooks`, `runtimeConfig`
- Runtime Modules:  `-`
- Build Modules:    `-`


### Reproduction

https://stackblitz.com/edit/nuxt-starter-l1dvnf?file=app.vue

### Describe the bug

There's actually two manifestations of this bug.

First bug:
- Given two pages, A & B, and two layouts, X and Y
- Page A uses Template X
- Page B uses Template Y
- When navigating to page A, it will mount the CSS for Template X
- When navigating to page B, it will mount the CSS for Template Y
- However, when navigating **_back_** to page A, it will not _remove_ the CSS for template Y.
- **Bug:** This means, effectively, that page A's rendering is unstable, and will render differently depending on preceding navigation.

Second bug:
- Given the above, if you use pre-fetching with `NuxtLink` (`<NuxtLink>` without `noPrefetch`), then the CSS for template Y will be injected into the page when navigating to page A, even though it has no association with Template Y.
- In other words, Nuxt eagerly injects CSS un-associated with the current page

Note that the first bug occurs whether or not you use `noPrefetch`.


### Additional context

I originally thought this bug was associated with / the same bug as https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/3877, but was told that was not the case, so filing this new issue. I also thought it might be the exact same as [this issue](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/13778), but that issue is closed?

### Logs

_No response_

comments.author: TheAlexLichter
comments.body:
@matthew-dean No, absolutely not! 😋

> Page A will keep the css files loaded from Page B after navigating B->A.

IMO This is expected and you can use `<style scoped>` (Scoped Styles) to avoid this. No styles will be "unloaded" when navigating. If your page has global styles that alter the whole application (non-scoped ones), they will stay throughout the user journey after being loaded unless somehow handled in userland ☺️

The same applies to the issue mentioned above I'd say.

[Fixed example using `:deep` + scoped styles](https://stackblitz.com/edit/nuxt-issues-22817).

---

Happy for some other opinions here though (cc @danielroe)

comments.author: danielroe
comments.body:
I agree with @manniL's take. You should not rely on whether a stylesheet is or isn't loaded. Nuxt may preload a stylesheet when the browser is idle, for example, to ensure that a page loads quickly and doesn't rely on additional network requests.

Vite may also bundle multiple pages' or layouts' CSS into a single file if they are very small.

These are implementation details.

Instead you should use scoped CSS, CSS modules, or unique selectors to ensure there are no conflicts. This is a matter of (IMO) best practice anyway.

comments.author: matthew-dean
comments.body:
I respectfully disagree, in that yes, it's understandable to preload assets, but
1. it's completely counter-intuitive to actually mount assets from components that are not themselves mounted, and mounting / preloading should not be conflated concepts
2. Simply using scoped CSS or CSS modules makes unfounded assumptions that Nuxt is being only used on sites that have been built entirely from scratch, and IMO worsens adoption for people migrating TO Nuxt.
3. Leaving a trail of unused CSS behind you, or mounting CSS that is not applied is not benign, and will have a progressively worsening impact on browser performance. To be fair, it's hard to know how large that impact is in modern browsers, but style recalculation is linear based on the number of selectors + amount of mounted markup.

Can we not enable an option to not pre-mount CSS? I tried [creating a custom Nuxt Link](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/discussions/23770), but there was no way to use `noPrefetch` in those options. For some reason, that option isn't exposed. I tried figuring out some kind of hook to manually remove the stylesheet from the DOM when a particular layout is unmounted, but I couldn't figure out a way to find an identifier that would allow me to query / remove CSS associated with a particular layout or component.

I understand the need to say no for edge cases, so I'm not saying you need to add this as a feature, but could you at least enable a way for me to do it? I feel like even those avenues are blocked.

comments.author: danielroe
comments.body: The behaviour here is not Nuxt's but Vite's; I would create a [proposal or feature request there](https://github.com/vitejs/vite), that we can then benefit from in Nuxt.

comments.author: wavedeck
comments.body:
> > Page A will keep the css files loaded from Page B after navigating B->A.
>
> IMO This is expected and you can use `<style scoped>`

While this is true for styles applied to individual pages, you cannot scope styles inside a layout, as this will not apply them to the pages using the layout.. so the only real workaround is to encapsulate the layout styles in another parent selector
(e.g. ".layout-a h1" and ".layout-b h1") or using completely unique selectors.

this issue drove me insane when i was trying to reduce css bundle size by splitting them into different layouts. The second you use NuxtLink without disabling prefetching, the styles will get combined again and can cause unexpected behaviour.

It also didn't help that this issue was closed, since it makes it more effort to find.

In general, I'm distressed that almost all of the major JavaScript SSR frameworks out there happen to have so many gotcha's when handling css. It's very hard to keep control and regularly lures me back to traditional SSR, where you have full control of the HTML for each page.

comments.author: matthew-dean
comments.body:
Note: I discovered today that this is also a problem for just page-to-page CSS, not just layout CSS. Navigating to a new page does not un-mount the CSS for a previous page. Therefore, if a page alters any CSS globals for that page, while the page is mounted, then those globals will persist long after the page is gone. I'm not sure why Nuxt would want the memory leak / performance issue of just endlessly stacking CSS while you navigate around. If you never refresh your page and navigate through 1,000 pages, won't you end up with 1,000 style tags trailing behind you? 🤔 

@manniL 

> No styles will be "unloaded" when navigating

Style tags are not benign if "un-used". The browser still has to build a style tree, and more styles means that takes longer, and it still has to traverse the DOM to know what tags have styles applied, which includes tags in the head. The DOM can (and will) degrade in performance the more elements are added. Leaving style trash in the wake of navigation just doesn't make a lot of sense.

comments.author: matthew-dean
comments.body:
I wrote a simple test with a Nuxt plugin, which looks like this:
```ts
import { defineNuxtPlugin } from '#app'

export default defineNuxtPlugin({
  name: 'css-register',
  hooks: {
    'page:loading:start'() {
      const styles = document.querySelectorAll('style')
      console.log('Number of styles:', styles.length)
    }
  }
})
```
I loaded a `/links` route.
> Number of styles: 13

I navigated to a `/groups` route
> Number of styles: 21

I navigated back to `/links`
> Number of styles: 22

I navigated back to `/groups`
> Number of styles: 23

Back to `/links`
> Number of styles 23 (okay, interesting)

Back to `/groups`
> Number of styles: 24

🙃

comments.author: Mateleo
comments.body:
@Kreeg Yes, nothing changed because it's a Vite related issue, not directly nuxt.
All three of these have to be true at once to trigger this bug:

1. You write global (non-scoped) styles inside a page or layout, a plain `<style>` block, not `<style scoped>`, targeting a shared selector like `body`, `html`, `:root`, or a generic `class`.
2. Two different routes set the same global selector to different values (e.g. layout X does` body { background: red }`, layout Y does `body { background: blue }`).
3. You navigate between them.

I have no idea how to fix this for Nuxt. Maybe an `experimental.cleanupStylesOnNavigation`

issues.title: transform `navigateTo` in `<script setup>` to provide an early return
issues.body:
### Environment

Nuxt project info:                                                                                                                                                                                                               1:53:15 PM

------------------------------
- Operating System: Linux
- Node Version:     v20.5.1
- Nuxt Version:     3.7.3
- CLI Version:      3.8.4
- Nitro Version:    2.6.3
- Package Manager:  yarn@1.22.19
- Builder:          -
- User Config:      devServer, vite, nitro, build, devtools, modules, css
- Runtime Modules:  @nuxt/devtools@0.6.7
- Build Modules:    -
------------------------------


### Reproduction

see https://github.com/bf/nuxt3-script-setup-await-navigateTo-bug

```
<script setup lang="ts">
await navigateTo("/a")
await navigateTo("/b")
</script>
```

expected: navigate to /a and stop there
observed: navigate to /a and then to /b/ and stop at /b

### Describe the bug

There's no way to terminate execution in `<script setup>` block. Previously `return navigateTo()` could be used but it has been deprecated (see https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/15002 ).

Now if I have business logic in the `<script setup>`, for example like this: 

```
<script setup>
const { data: milk, error: errorMilk } = await useFetch("/api/milk")

if (errorMilk.value) {
	throw errorMilk.value
}

if (milk.value && milk.value.length === 0) {
	await navigateTo("/a")
}

const { data: honey, error: errorHoney } = await useFetch("/api/honey")

if (errorHoney.value) {
	throw errorHoney.value
}

if (honey.value && honey.value.length === 0) {
	await navigateTo("/b")
}
</script>
```

It will not terminate at the `(milk.value && milk.value.length === 0)` and navigate to `/a` but it will first navigate to `/a` and later to `/b`.

Generally, there should be a way to stop execution in script setup and navigate to another page.

### Additional context

Also tried with 
```
<script setup lang="ts">
await navigateTo("/a", { replace: true, external: true})
await navigateTo("/b", { replace: true, external: true})
</script>
```
and
```
<script setup lang="ts">
await navigateTo("/a", { replace: true})
await navigateTo("/b", { replace: true})
</script>
```
but in all cases it navigates to '/b' and not '/a'

### Logs

_No response_

issues.title: Use custom runtime environmental variables (instead of NUXT_ prefix)
issues.body:
### Describe the feature

Refering to [runtime configuration ](https://nuxt.com/docs/guide/going-further/runtime-config#environment-variables), I think that the current implementation (runtime variables will be overriden by NUXT_ prefixed environmental viariables) is kind of ugly. 
The problem is that one may already have some env vars, e.g. (DB_URL), that might live in a common env file that is shared among many applications. With the current implementation we have to "pollute" the env file with duplicate definitions (e.g. add the NUXT_DB_URL in addition to the already existing, duplicating the variable content as well).

While, nuxt could just have a semantic to resolve arbitrary env vars (at runtime). e.g.
```
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  runtimeConfig: {
    apiSecret: '${APP_SECRET}' // This resolves the environment variable APP_SECRET at runtime
```


Using
```
nuxt version 3.6.5
```


### Additional information

- [ ] Would you be willing to help implement this feature?
- [ ] Could this feature be implemented as a module?

comments.author: robbyemmert
comments.body:
Not controlling the environment variable scheme is a PAIN on many projects.

For example, Neon's Vercel integration, and Github Actions, inject several environment variables (DATABASE_URL, GITHUB_TOKEN) which we have no control over. 

Developers and AI agents alike are totally confused why environment variables are not available at runtime. And I have to say, this is basic Node functionality that somehow is broken in Nuxt.

IMO a better way to get the same security without the annoyance and inoperability is:
- Don't make sensitive variables available at build time.
- Don't bundle process.env into the front end (this makes a ton of sense, and is already the case).
- Access process.env anywhere in the server at runtime to get access to environment variables (like a normal Node app)
- If you want a unified config, simply make one, or register your env vars in nuxt.config.ts

You should be able to do:
```ts
}
  // ...
  runtimeConfig: {
    myVar: process.env.MY_VAR
  }
}
```

^^^ This not working confuses everyone. I get that env vars override this, but that is backwards from how most people think. IMO a framework like this shouldn't force people to re-think how they code, but should simply accelerate or augment existing conventions. There are lots of ways to control env vars (i.e. with turbo) outside of nuxt if you want the added security. Otherwise, it's just an annoyance.

Just my 2 cents.

comments.author: Rigo-m

Let's say you have `/api/fetchSomething.ts` that takes 10 whole seconds to fetch that data.
You then move to `routeRules` and you set `{ '/api/fetchSomething': { prerender: true }`

At that point, that API gets prerendered and transformed as a plain text file during your build, **but**:
- If you fetch that route externally or during CSR: instant response with the prerendered content ensues (yay! 🎉 )
- If you have a useFetch inside a component setup, and that component/page gets SSR, the expensive computation gets called (so the page takes 10+ seconds to render

issues.title: Inconsistencies when using multiple hybrid renderings
issues.body:
### Environment

------------------------------
- Operating System: Linux
- Node Version:     v18.17.1
- Nuxt Version:     3.8.2
- CLI Version:      3.10.0
- Nitro Version:    2.8.1
- Package Manager:  pnpm@8.11.0
- Builder:          -
- User Config:      devtools, routeRules
- Runtime Modules:  -
- Build Modules:    -
------------------------------

### Reproduction

You can check the following repo: https://github.com/mitjans/nuxt-route-rules
Then, you can:

1. Build the application: `nuxt build`
2. Serve the application: `node .output/server/index.mjs`
3. Send requests with [httpie](https://httpie.io/cli):
  `http :3000/spa`
4. Check if the page is being rendered in the client or the server by looking at the node server's console logs and the httpie response (if the page comes rendered or not)

### Describe the bug

I've set up a simple Nuxt app with the following Nuxt config (and pages):

```typescript
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  ssr: false,
  routeRules: {
    "/static": { static: true },
    "/prerendered": { prerender: true },
    "/ssr": { ssr: true },
    "/spa": { ssr: false },
  },
});
```

Things I've noticed:

- **❓[QUESTION]:**  What happens when global `ssr: false` but a route-rule sets a specific `ssr: true`. My guess is that the global `ssr` has more priority and so the poge `/ssr`, although specified to be rendered in the server, will be rendered as an SPA in the client. This behavior is reproducible in the provided Nuxt app. Would be nice to have some explicit mention of this in the documentation.
- **⁉️[QUESTION + POSSIBLE BUG]:** `static: true` is not listed in [the documentation](https://nuxt.com/docs/guide/concepts/rendering#route-rules). What's its effect? My guess:
  - When global or route `ssr: true`, it is hydrated at build time and served statically from the server
  - When global or route `ssr: false`, an HTML SPA application is created at build time, served statically, and hydrated on the client
  > 👆 if this is the case, it is not what I've been able to reproduce in the provided Nuxt app. In the first case, I see a `console.log('static page')` in the server, which means it is being hydrated in the server (?).
- **❗[POSSIBLE BUG]:** when `prerendered: true`, I would expect the page to be hydrated at build time and served statically (like the first case in the previous point), regardless of the global or route `ssr` setting. This behavior is not reproducible in the provided Nuxt app:
  - When `ssr: false`: the page is served as an SPA (hydrated in the client)
  - When `ssr: true`: the page is correctly hydrated at build time and served statically

Overall, my feeling is that there's a lack of documentation on how the rendering modes interact with each other. I would love to help and contribute to adding the missing documentation, but would like to first fully comprehend what's the expected behavior in each of the previous cases.

### Additional context

_No response_

### Logs

_No response_

issues.title: `useRouteParams` and `useRouteQuery` for Nuxt
issues.body:
### Describe the feature

Especially when it comes to handling URL state, I've seen the wildest implementations.
It would be great to have two simple helper composables which create "reactive" router params and router query values.
That way, it would be even easier to sync URL state (and we could properly document + advise it).

This [already exists in VueUse](https://vueuse.org/router/useRouteParams/) but does not utilize `navigateTo`.

Example syntax (adapted from VueUse example)

```ts
const search = useRouteQuery('search')

const otherSearch = useRouteQuery('search', 'foo') // default value

const page = useRouteQuery('page', '1', { transform: Number }) // with transform function too

console.log(search.value) // same as route.query.search
search.value = 'foobar' // Calls navigateTo({ query: { search: 'foobar' } }, { replace: true })
```

---

Related issue (was more bare-bone): https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/24365

### Additional information

- [X] Would you be willing to help implement this feature?
- [X] Could this feature be implemented as a module?

### Final checks

- [X] Read the [contribution guide](https://nuxt.com/docs/community/contribution).
- [X] Check existing [discussions](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/discussions) and [issues](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues).

comments.body:
Having some native `useRouteParams()` & co has been on my mind for a while but I haven't been able to dedicate it the time and energy it requires for an RFC, especially because of different flavors and the fact it can fully exist in userland. There are a lot of possibilities and options (push/replace, preserve params, query, serializer) so an RFC would be crucial to keep the implementation lean, flexible, and future proof with typed routes (unplugin-vue-router). I would advise **not to directly add this to Nuxt** to avoid any possible conflicts in the future. Instead, going through an RFC to add them to the router would benefit more people and ensure a better version for the future.

Regarding `navigateTo()`: I don't know what are the implications of using `router.push()` while the app is running. I know that it can be used in some extra places and adds redirect codes but I imagine it has no impact when executed while the app is already running, which is when these composables (useRouteParams(), etc) would be used.

Feel free to start an RFC as I won't have the time for it in the forseeable future

issues.title: `$fetch`: use `useRequestFetch()` when calling internal API during SSR
issues.body:
### Describe the feature

When having API routes in Nuxt with authentication (using H3 `useSession` or [nuxt-auth-utils](https://github.com/atinux/nuxt-auth-utils)), we need to forward the `cookie` to the API routes when fetching the data on SSR.

### Not working

```vue
<script setup>
const { data: teams } = await useAsyncData('team', () => $fetch('/api/teams')
</script>
```

### Working

```vue
<script setup>
const { data: teams } = await useAsyncData('team', () => useRequestFetch()('/api/teams')
</script>
```

Or using `useFetch`:

```vue
<script setup>
const { data: teams } = await useFetch('/api/teams', { key: 'teams' })
</script>
```

I believe it should work when we call our Nuxt API directly with `$fetch` to improve the DX.

### Additional information

- [X] Would you be willing to help implement this feature?
- [ ] Could this feature be implemented as a module?

### Final checks

- [X] Read the [contribution guide](https://nuxt.com/docs/community/contribution).
- [X] Check existing [discussions](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/discussions) and [issues](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues).
issues.author: atinux

comments.author: pi0
comments.body:
This is a nice idea to improve DX, considering cases where users are directly using `$fetch` for this purpose of passing header however I'm afraid it reduces the portability of `fetch` and `$fetch` if we do an implicit behavior like this (ie: a utility can work in ambient context and plugins while broken in the lifecycle of a request with invalid headers or wise-versa also behavior in server-routes which worth to consider further discussion in Nitro if we wanna do something like this.)

I would suggest alternatively this to be shipped as part of factory function fetches. We could introduce also a preconfigured `$apiFetch` version that is intended for end-users explicitly and can contain additional logic like this. We can also introduce a new composable like `$fetchWithHeaders` that depends on context.

comments.body:

Also, this should really be documented.

comments.author: moriloop
comments.body:
How to handle this issue more generally and what should be done when we don't use fetch directly?!

Assume that we are using an SDK function in `useAsyncData` and this function uses its own version of `fetch`. For example: 

```js
<script setup>
const { data: userProfile } = await useAsyncData('user-profile', () => $api.getCurrentUser())
</script>
```
Assuming that login has already been performed and the appropriate `cookie` exists, the above function works correctly on the client-side. However, it encounters problems during server-side rendering. As @Atinux sayed we need to forward the browser's cookies to the API routes when fetching the data (our performing any request) on SSR.

**In general**, any information present in the context of a page request, including `headers` and `cookies`, that triggers the SSR process should be propagated to every request made within that page using the fetch API.
This aligns with the developer's perspective since they perceive all fetch calls as originating from the browser, which automatically includes headers and cookies. 

Dear  @danielroe and @pi0 , I would appreciate your thoughts on this matter. Also, what are some current solutions for the example I mentioned? That is, when using an SDK and not having direct access to fetch, what should we do to avoid SSR issues?

danielroe
comments.body: @moshetanzer No, that won't pass on the request details. In fact, useFetch passes on the request details by default and you are overriding _not_ to do it. I would suggest you open a new issue to discuss as it's not exactly relevant to this one.

```sh
http-server -p 5550 --cors
```

```ts
import { externalLoader } from './external-loader';
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  vite: {
    plugins: [externalLoader()],
```

```ts
import { Plugin } from 'vite';
declare function externalLoader(): Plugin;
```

issues.body: ### Describe the feature I have encountered an issue where users expect that when there's a error on the page, the correct content can still be displayed so they can access other useful information. Currently, as soon as an error occurs in the application, it redirects to a custom error page, which leaves users feeling confused. I really hope that Nuxt can provide a configuration option to disable the display of the error component within `nuxt-root.vue` . This allows the rest of the page to be displayed normally if there are no errors, rather than having the entire page turn into an error page. It would be a significant loss if a minor error within a component resulted in the entire page being inaccessible. There is a desire for a feature that allows the behavior to be the same as Vue's original error handling in applications. (Below are two contrasting examples.) Thank you. ### Examples The components are structurally consistent and the application includes an error handling function, yet they exhibit significant differences in performance.
